issues.legal_issue: Education is not by itself a charitable purpose for property-tax exemption where the educational activity is not predominantly directed to charitable ends rather than earning profit.
material_facts: A society ran a recognized private unaided school in a building it owned.
The school collected fees and generated recurring surpluses; the society’s only activity was running the school.
The Court held that imparting education alone did not establish that the property was used for a charitable purpose.
issues.conclusion: Education may be a charitable purpose, but educational activity alone does not establish a charitable purpose for the exemption; the predominant object must be charitable rather than profit-making.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 115(4)(a) and its Explanation of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, education is included within charitable purpose, but it is not automatically charitable when conducted with a profit motive. The Court applied the principle that the predominant object must serve charity, not earn profit, relying on Special Commissioners of Income Tax v. Pemsel; The King v. The Commissioners for Special Purposes of the Income Tax; The Abbey, Malvern Wells, Ltd. v. Minister of Town and Country Planning; The Trustees of the Tribune; All India Spinners’ Association v. Commissioner of Income-Tax; Commissioner of Income-Tax, Bombay City v. Breach Candy Swimming Bath Trust; and Addl. C.I.T., Gujarat v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association. The Court noted that the statutory definition was narrower than the Income Tax Act’s definition.

rule.if: property_tax_exemption_claim and education_activity and not predominant_charitable_object

predicates.property_tax_exemption_claim: A society or body seeks exemption from property tax for land or a building it occupies and uses.
predicates.education_activity: The society or body uses the property to impart education.
predicates.predominant_charitable_object: The predominant object of the activity is to serve a charitable purpose rather than to earn profit.

issues.definition: When a property-tax exemption is claimed for educational use but the activity’s predominant object is not charitable, educational use alone does not establish a charitable purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A society qualifies as supported wholly or in part by voluntary contributions only when it substantially depends on genuinely voluntary contributions for its maintenance, rather than being able to sustain itself from its own income.
material_facts: The school society’s income included fees collected from students, and it generated recurring surpluses.
The school transferred funds to the society, but the school and society were under the same control; the Court held that those transfers were not voluntary contributions to the society.
The evidence did not establish that the society depended on substantial voluntary contributions for its support.
In the other appeal, the Corporation challenged the view that receipt of even a small voluntary contribution was enough to satisfy the statutory test.
issues.conclusion: The test is quantitative as well as qualitative: the society must depend on an appreciable, substantial amount of voluntary contributions for its sustenance. A society that can support itself without them does not qualify, even if it applies its income to charitable objects and does not distribute profits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115(4)(a) and its proviso require that the society be supported wholly or in part by voluntary contributions, apply its profits or other income to promoting its objects, and pay no dividend or bonus to its members. “Support” means sustenance or maintenance; “part” means an appreciable and substantial part, not an insignificant amount. Contributions made under compulsion or in expectation of an advantage are not voluntary, and transfers between a school and the society controlling it are not voluntary contributions. Although the general tax is annual, the Court said the reasonable approach is to assess dependence over a five-year period and review it thereafter.

rule.if: property_tax_exemption_claim and society_support_claim and not substantial_voluntary_support

predicates.property_tax_exemption_claim: A society or body claims property-tax exemption for land or a building occupied and used for its purposes.
predicates.society_support_claim: The society or body claims that it is supported wholly or in part by voluntary contributions.
predicates.substantial_voluntary_support: The society substantially depends for its maintenance on appreciable contributions that are genuinely voluntary.

issues.definition: A society claiming exemption on the basis of charitable use is not entitled to it when it does not substantially depend on genuinely voluntary contributions for maintenance.

issues.legal_issue: When a building includes a distinct portion used for trade or business or from which rent is derived, that portion is treated separately for municipal taxation, and the charitable use of another portion does not itself exempt it.
material_facts: A charitable trust owned a building containing portions occupied by a press and other portions used for the trust’s activities.
The press occupied identified areas of the building, and rent was derived from property use.
The dispute included whether the press-occupied areas could be exempt along with the other portions.
issues.conclusion: The trade or rental portion is separately subject to tax; the remaining portion may be considered separately for exemption if it independently satisfies the statutory conditions.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 115(5) and 115(6) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 provide that land or buildings, or portions of them, are not treated as exclusively occupied and used for charitable purposes where trade or business is carried on or rent is derived, and that an exempt portion is treated as a separate property for municipal taxation. The Court also explained that a trade or business may serve as a means to a charitable end where its profits are applied to charity and no part is distributed to members; the portions are assessed separately.

predicates.property_tax_exemption_claim: A society or body claims property-tax exemption for a building or part of a building.
predicates.identifiable_trade_or_rental_portion: An identifiable portion of the property is used for trade or business or produces rental income.

issues.definition: When an identifiable portion of property is used for trade or business or produces rent, that portion is subject to tax separately from any other portion that may qualify for exemption.
